completes without abort) re-subscribes for free and never spends the
budget, its stream-ended telemetry journaling once per stop rather than
once per close (an aborted exit stays silent).

# Design invariants

- **Fail-open vs BLOCKED.** Enforcement is fail-open: every hook body journals
  internal errors and proceeds, and the plugin always loads. Only `BlockError`
  reaches the host, and only from deliberate gate decisions, which throw
  `BLOCKED by turnstile:`.
- **Parent-keyed state.** Reads, round counts, and gate flags count against
  the parent, resolved asynchronously via `childToParent`; unresolved edges
  journal a fallback signal rather than mis-keying.
- **Provenance-scoped, stage-aware waivers.** `USER WAIVER:` / `PLAN APPROVED:`
  are honored only from the user's own prompt (hook or inbox stream, deduped
  by message id); agent-composed dispatch prompts containing those literals
  are inert. Waiver scope is literal configured stage names, not intent
  parsing: the configured agent names named in the waiver text scope it to
  those stages' gates (the plan gate is covered by either the plan-reviewer
  or executor name); an unscoped waiver covers every gate but the reviewer
  gate consumes it on the first dispatch it unlocks, and a scoped waiver
  stays live until that stage's waiver allowance is spent, metered separately
  from the ordinary dispatch caps. The family rides the same one-prompt
  replay grace (a restart resume or a `continuationCarry` re-admission) and
  is otherwise dropped on a new prompt. One exception to "covers every
  gate": the landing gate never consults the waiver. `git push` is released
  only by the credited reviewer `VERDICT: APPROVE` or the human permission
  ask, so a waiver aimed at landing is captured at admission and inert at
  that gate.
- **Latest-wins markers.** A `GATE: FAIL` un-greens an earlier PASS, within
  and across texts; dedup is per parent with first-sight provenance;
  cross-child duplicate observations are suppressed (counted, not silently
  dropped).
- **Fail-toward-strict on stale evidence.** Stale approvals are invalidated
  rather than trusted: a bound approval goes stale when its own plan is
  edited (`plan-edited`) or removed (`plan-missing`); an unbound approval
  goes stale on any plans-dir content-signature change
  (`signature-mismatch`). Restart grace survives exactly one prompt
  (`replayGrace`).
- **Marker drift is mechanically checked.** The marker regexes in
  `src/markers.ts`, the examples in `README.md`, the `docs/usage.md` index,
  and `agents/*.md`, the policy prose in `src/policy.ts`, and
  `scripts/evidence.mjs`'s MARKER_OK copy are validated together by
  `scripts/check-markers.mjs` (wired into `npm run ci`), including negative
  probes that reject near-miss marker text.

# Persistence: journal and restart

![Journal and replay](../images/d05-persistence.svg)

The journal is the plugin's only persistence edge. It lives outside the
repo at `~/.local/share/opencode/metrics/`. The store is a shared
`turnstile.jsonl` plus a per-session `sessions/<parentID>.jsonl` sink
(`journalPerSession`, default on). `gate-events.log` (trace only),
`anchors.jsonl`, and `approved-plans.jsonl` sit beside them. Retention is
bounded: 5 MB per file, 5 generations per file. `replayTailLines` (default 2000) bounds the boot window.

On restart, `replayGatePasses` (`src/ledger.ts`) walks the generations
newest-first. It merges by `ts` and folds last-wins per session. It
restores gate flags, verdicts, ensemble counts, the observe period, and
the suspension map. The `prov:stated` / `prov:denied` / `prov:waiver` /
`prov:override` decision-ledger rows ride the same journal. Every read
error is fail-open: the journaler records it and never throws.

The full catalog lives in [journal/entry-types.md](../journal/entry-types.md). It lists every entry
type with its replay fold, the file layout, rotation
mechanics, and the tamper-evidence hash chain.

# Policy injection

Turnstile does not read orchestrator policy from a file at install time; it
makes that policy available by injecting it at runtime. The primary channel is
the pre-first-model-call `session.context` hook: `injectContextPolicy` in
`src/context-surface.ts` appends the policy head (and any pending intent nudge)
into the parent's primary-turn draft `system` array before the first model
call, parent-guarded and latched (see the `context` hook in [hooks](hooks.md)). The
`execute.after` body in `src/hooks-tool.ts` stays armed as the fallback: it
prepends the orchestrator policy paragraph from `src/policy.ts` (via
`src/delivery.ts`) to the first `task` (or `subagent`) result delivery per
task, once per task, and appends a per-delivery `PIPELINE:` status tail to
every
pipeline-stage delivery (see Pipeline continuation below), via the
`tool.hook("execute.after")` handler (the same hook the plugin already uses
to rewrite tool output reaching the model). Each
delivery is classified once by `classifyDelivery` into its host shape: the
v1 string shape (child-keyed event, text in `result.output`, the child
optionally named by a string `metadata.sessionID`) or the v2 structured shape
(parent-keyed event, structured `result.output`, the child on
`metadata.sessionID` or the structured `output.sessionID`, the canonical
child text in `output.output`, model-visible `content` as a string or a block
array). The policy head and the status tail both land on that shape's
model-visible text through the shared shape ladder (`mutateDeliveryText`):
`result.output` for the string shape; string or block-array `result.content`
for the structured one (a string carries both mutations in place, a block
array gains one prepended head block and one appended tail block, and absent
or other content falls back to the structured output string, which the host
stringifies into the transcript).
The classified child and text also drive marker parsing, the bare-output
check, and the reviewer capture, always from the canonical `output.output`
string, so a structured delivery parses and attributes to the real child
exactly like its string twin. Attribution is
edge-first: the `childToParent` edge (seeded by `session.created`, back-filled
via `session.get` in `resolveParent`) decides where the policy lands, so both
shapes inject on the receiving parent; the `policyInjected` flag and the
`injected:true` journal entry key on that resolved parent. The source of truth
is code shipped with the plugin, so a fresh install can never lose it, and it
follows the plugin through updates and uninstall–reinstall cycles.

- **Fail-open.** The injection is fully guarded with an inner try/catch; on
  failure it journals a `type:"policy"` entry with `injected:false` and
  proceeds, so a broken injection never blocks a tool call ([invariants](invariants.md)). The status
  tail has its own fail-open catch: a throwing append journals
  `{type:"error", error:"pipeline-status: …"}` without rethrowing, and the
  independent policy head still lands (and vice versa). The only silent skips
  are the once-flag (which gates only the policy head; the tail lands on
  every pipeline-stage delivery) and an absent result (nothing to deliver);
  a present-but-unclassifiable result journals loudly on EVERY such delivery
  (the once-flag no longer gates it) as
  `{type:"policy", injected:false, reason:"unknown-shape", shape:<descriptor>}`,
  where the descriptor is a
  bounded, value-free summary of the unrecognized result (per-field types
  plus the sorted key names of an object `output`, capped at 8), so a broken
  shape is discoverable by grepping `type:"policy"` like every other skip.
- **Per-task idempotency.** A `GateState.policyInjected` flag (cleared on
  each new prompt, so the block re-injects per task) means the policy is
  prepended exactly once per task, not once per turn. The `PIPELINE:` tail
  has no such once-flag; it is per-delivery by design. The shared latch also
  gates the context-hook channel: its success journals
  `{type:"policy", injected:true, surface:"context"}` and its skips journal
  `skipped:true` with reason `context-agent` / `context-child` /
  `context-no-id`, discoverable by grepping `type:"policy"` like every other
  decision.
- **Pipeline continuation.** Every pipeline-stage delivery (the delivery's
  agent matched against the configured `config.agents` names, so a renamed
  install names its renamed stages) gains a one-line status tail rendered
  by `formatPipelineStatus` (`src/state.ts`) from the resolved parent's gate
  state after the just-arrived delivery: `PIPELINE: <stage>=done
plan=APPROVED|PENDING tests=GREEN|RED reviewer=<n>/2 next=<successor> —
<directive>`. The successor is the stage the orchestrator dispatches next,
  decidable from the gate flags alone: planner → plan-reviewer; plan-reviewer
  → executor once `hasPlanVerdict` holds, else planner (a BLOCK re-plans);
  executor → test-runner; test-runner → reviewer once `hasGatePass` holds,
  else executor (a FAIL re-runs); reviewer → the literal `land` once
  `hasReviewApprove` holds, else the reviewer again while `reviewerDispatches`
  is below `REVIEW_ENSEMBLE_SIZE` (2), else the literal `escalate`. The
  directive is "dispatch the next agent in this same turn" for a stage
  successor, "task complete; land through the gated push" for `land`, and
  "escalate to the user" for `escalate`. Two documented residuals: an agent
  outside the five stages renders `""` and the append is skipped entirely
  (non-pipeline deliveries stay byte-identical); and on a capped round (the
  other legs carry dispatch caps too: planner 3, plan-reviewer 3,
  test-runner 4) the line may name a stage the dispatch gate will refuse;
  it reports the pipeline's nominal successor, not the gate's cap check. The
  tail rides the policy head's `mutateDeliveryText` shape ladder, and the
  output always reads policy head → child text → `PIPELINE:` tail (the
  once-per-load `[turnstile] config:` block sits between head and child text,
  per the config-surface ordering). Every status word is a non-marker token,
  so an echoed copy of the line never parses as a `GATE:`/`VERDICT:` marker,
  and the line never enters the journal: persistence schema, replay,
  rotation, and `opencode-turnstile status` are unchanged.
- **Edge-first attribution.** A delivery whose child→parent edge is
  registered injects regardless of the `event.agent` name; the name
  heuristic never excludes an edge-resolved delivery. The name guard survives
  only as a conservative fallback for non-structured deliveries: a delivery
  carrying a config-known subagent name whose edge is unresolvable (no
  `session.created` and no `session.get` record) is skipped and journaled
  `{type:"policy", sessionID:<child>, injected:false, skipped:true,
reason:"agent-name"}` so the decision is observable. Structured deliveries
  skip the guard by construction: the host builds that result on the
  parent's own tool call, so it is always the parent-facing channel and
  `event.agent` there is the parent's agent name. Consulting it risks a
  bogus skip for a parent running under a config-known name. The one
  residual corner that still injects without an edge is a config-UNKNOWN
  name on a host without a session API:
  with neither an edge nor a name signal there is no way to tell a
  parent-facing delivery from a child-own session one, so the self-keyed
  injection there is a documented, accepted residual. The handler fires only
  on `task`/`subagent` tool results, so child streaming text never receives
  the policy.
- **Marker placeholders.** The injected paragraph quotes the gate/verdict
  markers with `<n>` placeholders (e.g. `GATE: PASS tests=<n> passed=<n>
failed=<n>`, `VERDICT: APPROVE crit=<n> high=<n> med=<n> low=<n>`) rather
  than concrete digits, and never the pipe-joined `PASS|FAIL` form. The
  plugin parses markers from _any_ session text but applies them only from a
  marker-contracted emitter, so a fully concrete example echoed back by an
  unauthoritative session is journaled `suppressed` rather than flipping a
  gate. The placeholder form stays unparseable, which is defense in depth
  against a contracted emitter echoing a fully concrete line (e.g. a reviewer
  re-stating a verdict) and against contract drift.
- **Per-agent instructions** are not injected by the plugin: they live in
  each `agents/<name>.md` installed alongside the plugin.

With the plugin **off**, none of this prose is present anywhere; there is no
AGENTS.md block to fall back on. That is the deliberate tradeoff: loss-proof
by construction while the plugin loads, and a known, documented gap when it
does not.

A legacy variant once wrote a managed contract block into
`~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`. That block is now orphaned: the plugin no
longer reads or manages it, and it will coexist with the injected policy
(duplicate prose until removed). There is deliberately no installer to remove
it; turnstile no longer owns that file, so it never rewrites it. Delete the
section between the `<!-- turnstile:start -->` and `<!-- turnstile:end -->`
sentinels by hand, once; after that, the injected policy is the single source
of orchestrator policy for the session.

# Positioning: how turnstile fits the ecosystem

Claude Code's agent workflows are backed by host-side governance:
permission prompts and tool hooks that can stop a call before it
happens. Turnstile brings that shape to OpenCode: gates the
runtime enforces, not requests the model honors. It borrows the
enforcement model without the implementation, and stays
OpenCode-native: zero dependencies, TypeScript, loaded from your own
checkout.

The baseline question is what OpenCode v2 already provides natively:
subagents, per-tool permission rules, and prompt instructions. Those
cover the steering half of a pipeline. The mechanical half rests on
three capabilities the native surface structurally cannot express, and
each maps to a turnstile mechanism:

- **Stateful, task-scoped gates.** Permission rules are stateless
  per-tool-call decisions; they cannot condition a dispatch on prior
  task state. Turnstile's `GateState` buckets (`src/state.ts`), keyed
  per parent session and reset per prompt, make "executor blocked until
  this task's plan is approved" and per-leg round caps expressible
  and decidable in `tool.hook("execute.before")`, outside the model
  loop.
- **Evidence correlation.** No host feature verifies a model's claim
  against actual tool history. `src/evidence.ts` correlates a
  `GATE: PASS` marker with a recorded exit-0 test execution matching
  `evidencePattern` (the default covers the canonical `npm run ci`
  verification chain) before the reviewer gate flips; a bare marker stays
  `unverifiedPass` and never greens the gate under
  `gateEvidence:"enforce"`. The correlation re-runs when a child→parent
  edge resolves late (a background dispatch) and at reviewer-dispatch
  time, bounded to the parent's current task window (a prompt-admission
  stamp), so a stale prior-task execution cannot verify a new task's
  claim; a gate-unverified refusal names the sessions it searched
  (parent plus every child with journaled executions, with attribution
  reasons) in the `BLOCKED` message and the `searched` field of the
  journaled `blocked` entry.
- **A decision journal.** OpenCode logs are diagnostics, not a
  structured decision record. `src/journal.ts` appends every gate
  transition, block, waiver, and dispatch to a replayable JSONL trail
  (`replayGatePasses`, `src/ledger.ts`), which is what makes gates
  reviewable after the fact and stateful across restarts.

The README's pitch states the same three properties in one screen for
arriving readers; this section is where a developer can see the mechanisms
behind them.

Most other agent-structure projects on OpenCode are orchestration
suites: an orchestrator plans work, dispatches specialists, and
reconciles results. Some add pipeline discipline on top, but the
discipline is carried by prompts: a phase header the model prints at
the start of a response, a "review gate" step inside a skill's
instructions, a warning when a write lands without a prior test run.
Those asks work when the model complies. Turnstile's gates aim a step
further: they are decided in tool and task-dispatch hooks, outside the
model loop, so a dispatch that violates a gate fails before a subagent
session is created.

Turnstile is a layer under orchestration suites, not a competitor: it
reads task dispatches to attribute markers and enforce gates; it never
plans work, routes models, or spawns specialists. An orchestration
suite that dispatches task calls with agent names will pass through
turnstile unchanged unless a gate applies. Other adjacent approaches
gate on written artifacts, like spec workflows, or on a single
human-approval point; turnstile gates the machine steps around those.
The bundled planner/executor/test-runner/reviewer agents in
`agents/` are the reference pipeline, not a requirement; the
gates key off agent names and markers, and other suites' agents can
carry their own markers.

Three properties matter for comparing enforcement layers, and all three
are visible in this repo's tests:

- Verifiable state. `GATE:` and `VERDICT:` markers are parsed from
  child session text (`src/markers.ts`), stored per parent session
  (`src/ledger.ts`), and replayed from the JSONL journal on restart, so
  replayed gate state survives a restart and the next user prompt; then
  every later prompt starts a clean gate cycle rather than living in a
  prompt.
- Failure posture. Hooks fail open ([invariants](invariants.md)): an internal error is journaled and
  the call proceeds. The only refusals are deliberate
  `BLOCKED by turnstile:` throws at a declared gate. A broken
  enforcement plugin should degrade to prompt contracts, not break
  every session.
- Auditability. Every dispatch, gate transition, verdict, and blocked
  call is appended to `turnstile.jsonl` (bounded rotation, see
  SECURITY.md). The journal is the record of what was claimed, which is
  what makes the gates reviewable after the fact.

The tradeoff is scope: turnstile is host-coupled to the OpenCode v2
plugin API and enforces exactly the
pipeline above. Multi-harness suites reach further; turnstile goes
deeper on one host and one pipeline.

# Security posture and limits

Turnstile is a speed bump and an audit trail, not a security boundary.

- Any text matching the gate marker, including a marker an agent
  hallucinated or copied from documentation, is journaled `verified:false`
  under the default `gateEvidence:enforce` mode and does not flip
  `hasGatePass` unless the current task's bash/shell executions contain a
  matching exit-0 test command (plausibility checked against
  `evidencePattern`; the default covers the canonical `npm run ci`
  verification chain). An agent that wants a green gate can no longer emit
  `GATE: PASS tests=1 passed=1 failed=0` without running anything. But
  `gateEvidence:flag` reverts to the historical flip-on-trust semantics
  (still stamped `verified:false`), and `gateEvidence:off` journals without
  the field at all.
- A `GATE: PASS` is only as trustworthy as the journal: an attacker who can
  write or replay the metrics directory can craft a `verified:true` entry,
  and `flag`/`off` make a fabricated marker trust-lossless. Tests that run
  outside the observable bash/shell surface (external CI, a differently
  named execution tool) leave enforce mode with no evidence to verify
  against; operators in that situation use `flag`/`off` at the cost of the
  guarantee. The journal records what was _claimed_, never proof.
- The dispatch-prompt waiver-forgery vector is closed: a `USER WAIVER:` (or
  `PLAN APPROVED:`) substring inside an agent-composed dispatch prompt
  unlocks nothing. Turnstile reads waivers and approvals only from the
  user's prompt at admission. The residual trust stance is unchanged: the
  journal is still the record of what was _claimed_ (an attacker who can
  write or replay the metrics directory can still craft entries), so the
  journal is treated as sensitive data (see SECURITY.md).
- `scripts/check-markers.mjs` guards against accidental drift between the
  parser and documented markers; it cannot guard against forgery, because
  the markers are plain prose by design.
- The `bash`/`shell`/`write`/`edit` denylist is a deterrent, not a sandbox: it
  matches strings, so `bash -c "$X"`, script files, `eval` indirection, and
  values sourced from the environment still bypass it. A block names the matched
  _rule_ (never the raw command, per the redaction contract); a dropped or
  invalid regex _source_ means the operation it guarded is now **allowed**
  (documented so a config typo weakens the policy visibly in the journal rather
  than silently). Both denylists default to empty, so none of this applies
  unless rules are configured, but gaps remain by design. `git` **aliases** (e.g. `git co main`,
  `git cm -m x`) are not matched, because a rule names `git` plus a literal
  subcommand only; and the wider base can _over-match_ (e.g. `git commit -m "…
merge …"` trips the `merge` rule). git/gh consent rides the host permission
  `ask` layer by default; a host `allow` never unblocks a configured turnstile
  deny, because the layers are complementary. `session_move` never blocks.
- MCP tools and other tool names not named in `execute.before` (`task`,
  `subagent`, `read`, `bash`, `shell`, `write`, `edit`, `session_move`) remain
  unguarded. Governing them is a follow-on, not part of this policy layer.

Use OpenCode's permission and sandboxing mechanisms against hostile agents.
Treat turnstile's journal as the record of what was _claimed_, and treat the
journal itself as sensitive data (see SECURITY.md).

There is no audit-only mode: every configured rule blocks. The opt-outs
are per-feature config keys: `gitGates.commitMessages: false` disables
commit lint, `gitGates.landingGate: false` disables the landing gate, an
empty denylist leaves the tool policy idle, and `TURNSTILE OFF:` (the
suspend marker) suspends all blocking session-wide. Legacy configs that
still carry `toolPolicy.mode`, `gitGates.mode`, or `handsOnGate` have
those keys dropped with a surfaced warning at load; the enforcement stays
on.

# A task, end to end

The three lifelines: orchestrator (parent session), child subagent sessions,
and the journal, the only persistence edge.

![Task flow](../images/d03-task-flow.svg)

A typical enforced run:

1. The user's prompt is admitted; a new task resets prior gate state (or
   carries earned flags across a continuation prompt with an unchanged
   worktree fingerprint).
2. The planner runs (subject only to loop caps); its `AC-n`/`chunk-N` plan
   lands in `.opencode/plans/`. With `requirementsPhase: true` a
   non-trivial task first dispatches the requirements subagent, whose spec
   (after the Open Questions round-trip) is passed verbatim into the planner
   dispatch (see [Requirements phase](gates.md#requirements-phase-opt-in-ungated)).
3. The plan-reviewer must APPROVE. A BLOCK dead-ends nothing: the plan is
   revised and re-review is attributed via round-scoped evidence (the newest
   dispatched plan-reviewer round wins within the parent).
4. The executor is gated on plan approval (keyed on the plan's **spec
   region**; the plan-approval row in [gates.md](gates.md) defines the hashing). Its result must
   cite `chunk-N` / `AC-n` entries from the decomposition. A **maintenance
   dispatch** (prompt declares maintenance scope for the live bound plan and
   the working-tree diff touches only non-src surfaces) rides a lighter
   path: it skips the plan-approval and decomposition gates and is capped at
   4 per plan. Eligibility is canonical in `src/maintenance.ts`; the journaling
   semantics are in [journal/entry-types.md](../journal/entry-types.md)'s `maintenance` entry.
5. The test-runner's `GATE: PASS` may require corroborating exit-0 bash
   evidence (`gateEvidence:"enforce"`); without it the flag is held as
   `unverifiedPass` and promoted when evidence arrives, including when a
   late child→parent edge back-fills the correlation, and only for
   executions journaled within the parent's current task window.
6. The reviewer's APPROVE credits the landing gate; under
   `reviewEnsemble:"enforce"` only after ≥2 unwaived reviewer dispatches.
7. `git push` is blocked until reviewer approval exists; the interactive
   landing ask arms immediately when the session carries a credited reviewer
   APPROVE that the prompt reset just dropped, and on a repeat push otherwise.

# Tamper evidence: the journal hash chain

When `tamperEvidence.enabled` is `true` (default `false`; the legacy
unchained row shape stays the default so existing journal consumers are
untouched), every journaled row carries three chain fields appended after
the payload: `seq` (per-file monotonic counter starting at 0), `prevHash`
(the previous row's hash, `""` for the first), and `hash`, the SHA-256 over
the canonical JSON (RFC 8785-style: sorted keys, no whitespace) of
`{prevHash, ts, payload}` (`src/chain.ts`, `node:crypto` only, zero runtime
dependencies). Editing, deleting, or reordering any row breaks every hash
after it.

Epochs batch the chain for verification and
[anchoring](anchors.md): every `epochEntries`
data rows (default 512, matching the rotation cadence) the journaler
appends a `chain-epoch` row, itself chained like any other, carrying
`{source, epoch, count, root, head}` where `root` is the Merkle root over
the epoch's data-row hashes (pairwise `sha256(a + b)`, an odd trailing node
hashed with itself, the single survivor hashed with itself once more) and
`head` is the epoch's last data-row hash. Two more entry types ride the
chain: `chain-epoch` (the commit above) and `chain-verify` (the session-end
verdict; verification is described below, anchor sinks in
[anchors.md](anchors.md)).

**Verification.** `verifyJournalChain` (`src/verify.ts`) folds every journal
file family (shared + per-session sinks) across its rotation generations
oldest-first, re-derives each row's hash and each epoch's Merkle root, and
reports the first broken link (`<family>:<line>: prevHash|seq|hash mismatch`
or an epoch root/head mismatch). Epoch indices are monotonic per family
across rotations: a seeding or resyncing journaler continues from the max
committed index in the surviving generations, so a `source#epoch` ref
identity is stable for the anchor cross-check. When rotation has pruned
generations (the oldest surviving file is a numbered generation other than
`.1`), its first chained row folds as a **trust root**: its `prevHash`
points into a pruned generation, so the prevHash continuity check is waived
for that row only (its own hash and a plausible `seq` are still verified).
When `tamperEvidence.verifyOnSessionEnd` is `true` (default `false`), the
session-idle handler runs it once per session and journals the
`chain-verify` verdict, toasting on failure, which shrinks the detection
window from "whenever someone runs the CLI" to one session. The same check
is available offline: `opencode-turnstile prov --verify` folds the chain
and verifies the epoch refs against the configured sinks, exiting 0 on an
intact anchored chain, 1 on the first broken link or any unanchored ref,
and 2 on usage errors.

Row-level inclusion proofs (`prov --verify --session <id>`) are described in
[anchors.md](anchors.md).

**Differential characterization** (integration-tested in
`tests/tamper-matrix.test.ts`): for each mutation of a captured honest
journal, built through the real write path with a rotation generation and a
task-completion anchor, the observed `prov --verify` verdict must equal the
characterized verdict, so a detector regression (false negative or false
positive) fails loudly:

| #   | Mutation                                                                                    | Expected result                                                                                                                       | Caught by                                                                                                                                            |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0   | none (control)                                                                              | verify passes                                                                                                                         | —                                                                                                                                                    |
| 1   | edit one row's payload                                                                      | fail, first broken link reported                                                                                                      | chain fold                                                                                                                                           |
| 2   | delete a row                                                                                | fail                                                                                                                                  | chain fold                                                                                                                                           |
| 3   | insert a fabricated row                                                                     | fail                                                                                                                                  | chain fold                                                                                                                                           |
| 4   | reorder rows                                                                                | fail                                                                                                                                  | chain fold / epoch root                                                                                                                              |
| 5   | fork (branch from an interior row)                                                          | fail                                                                                                                                  | chain fold / epoch root                                                                                                                              |
| 6   | rewrite-all with recomputed chain                                                           | chain folds clean, anchor check fails                                                                                                 | anchor                                                                                                                                               |
| 7   | edit rows within the un-anchored tail                                                       | **passes** (documented residual hole, bounded by the anchor cadence)                                                                  | —                                                                                                                                                    |
| 8   | truncate-and-continue (recurring-cleaner attack: truncate, keep logging into a fresh chain) | fail: previously published epoch roots become underivable from the current file, even though the new chain folds clean and re-anchors | anchor (CLI surfaces it via the unanchored-ref check against the retained store; missing-root detection confirmed at the `verifyJournalChain` level) |
| 9   | commit a wrong epoch root (row re-hashed honestly)                                          | fail: the per-record fold stays clean, so only the epoch-root check catches it                                                        | chain fold / epoch root                                                                                                                              |

Row 7 is deliberate: characterizing what the mechanism _cannot_ see is part
of the verification. Its scope is bounded by the anchoring trigger:
anything written after the last task-completion/session-end anchor is
unverifiable until the next one; if the anchor cadence changes,
re-characterize row 7.
Row 8 differs from a mid-file deletion (row 2): the surviving file is
internally valid from a new genesis, so only the anchor comparison catches
it. The harness also confirms a second task-completion anchor after the
truncation re-anchors the fresh chain without masking row 8's failure.
Row 9 isolates the epoch-root limb specifically: the tampered `chain-epoch`
row is re-hashed honestly, so rows 1–5's per-record detection is bypassed by
construction and the mismatch is attributable to the root/head check alone.
Integrity ≠ fidelity: a chain-valid journal that recorded fabricated
execution hashes fine and passes every row; detecting that class needs
ground-truth correlation outside the journal (out of scope here).

**Honesty caveats.** Integrity is not fidelity: the chain proves the
journal bytes are unchanged since they were written; it cannot prove the
_content_ was true (a gate that lied at write time hashes just as cleanly).
Detection latency is bounded by verification, not by chaining: an attacker
who controls the host can recompute the whole chain and forge the
host-domain `session-state` anchor too. Only the repo- and external-domain
sinks raise the cost above "edit two files", and nothing here stops a
determined host-level adversary (that is the tamper matrix's problem, out
of scope here).

Deletion and rotation semantics: anchor refs outlive the rows they vouch
for, so absence detection keys on the committed root (with the monotonic
epoch index as a bound), not on the ref's presence in the fold. An anchored
ref is reported absent only when its root matches no retained epoch AND its
index is at or above the family's lowest retained index, meaning a gap
within, or truncation of, retained history. An anchored epoch whose commit
row has rotated out entirely is satisfied silently: after that row is
pruned, absence is undetectable, the same trust domain as journal deletion.
Steady-state `verify` exit 0 is the expected signal; a red verify means
either genuine truncation within retained history or a store/journal
mismatch worth investigating.

One deletion caveat remains: because pruning makes the oldest surviving
generation's first row a trust root, deleting the oldest generations resets
the chain root, the same trust domain as deleting the journal outright. And
verify over an empty or wholly deleted journal with an empty anchor store
is vacuously ok: absence of rows is not evidence of integrity, which is why
the anchors live in a second file (or sink domain) that still names the
epochs the deleted journal should have contained. With anchors retained,
that deletion is exactly what the absence check reports.

# Journal file layout

## File layout

- **`turnstile.jsonl`** — the shared, always-on audit trail. Entries without
  a resolvable parent sessionID land here.
- **`sessions/<parentID>.jsonl`** — the per-session sink (the default, when
  `journalPerSession` is on). Every entry with a resolvable parent sessionID
  (via the ledger's `parentOf` map) appends here instead of the shared file,
  so one session's dispatches, verdicts, gates, blocks, and waivers read
  top-to-bottom in one file. Entries without a sessionID, or with an ID
  failing the session-ID shape rule, land in the shared `turnstile.jsonl`.
- **`gate-events.log`** — human-readable trace, only when `trace:true`.
- **`anchors.jsonl`** — the session-state anchor store, written only when
  `tamperEvidence.enabled` is `true` (see [tamper evidence: the hash
  chain](chain.md) and [anchors](anchors.md)). One published epoch ref per
  line, appended by the `session-state`
  sink at the task-completion and session-end triggers.
- **`approved-plans.jsonl`** — the durable approved-plan store (beside the
  journal by default; the factory's injected option redirects it). Each line
  is one record: a plan file name, its content key, and the project scope
  the approval was recorded under (derived from the resolved project
  directory).

  New records carry a `scheme: "spec"` tag; the key is the plan's
  spec-region sha256. A record without the tag was written under the legacy
  whole-file scheme, or an unknown newer scheme. A record covers a plan when
  its key equals the file's spec-region key or its whole-file key; then the
  plan is not pending. The whole-file key is the sha256 of the file's bytes
  at the current plans scan. A cached scan may reflect the bytes at its last
  refresh rather than the current file: a progress-only edit leaves the
  spec region (and the cached scan signature) unchanged, so a legacy record
  can be honored across such an edit, and the re-key it performs writes the
  current spec key.

  The first legacy match is transparently re-keyed to the current scheme:
  in-memory, sidecar append, and one replay-inert `plan-rekey` journal row
  with `reason: "durable-key-scheme"`. A record matching neither key leaves
  the plan pending with cause `durable-key-stale`: the enforcing dispatch
  journals the blocked row with that reason and a recovery message (one
  re-approval re-keys it) instead of the `no-plan-verdict` never-approved
  message.

  At boot the ledger loads the store. A missing file is a silent empty;
  another read error is journaled once and degrades to empty. The in-memory
  map is last-wins per (project, plan), capped at 256 records, and rewritten
  on eviction.

  A record is written when a _bound_ plan-reviewer APPROVE credits the gate.
  An unbound approval records nothing: human releases, prompts naming no
  single plan, a reviewer approval whose dispatch named no resolvable plan.

  A plan whose name and content key still match a record under the current
  project is not _pending_: the plan gate stays green for it even after the
  journal's APPROVE line has aged out of the replay window and across prompt
  resets. The exemption is re-derived from the sidecar, not the session
  bucket. A dispatch whose resolved plan is not pending is exempt even while
  unrelated plans stay pending.

  A record restores no session bucket itself (`hasPlanVerdict` and kin
  remain replay-only). An edited or replaced plan (content-key mismatch) or
  another project's plan stays pending. Read or write failures are
  fail-open: journaled, never blocking.

# Journal replay on restart

## Replay on restart

On restart, `replayGatePasses` (`src/ledger.ts`) walks the shared journal
generations newest-first (`turnstile.jsonl`, then `.1`, `.2`, … while the
file exists), then every `sessions/` file family's generations the same
way. The directory read is guarded: any failure replays the shared file
only. Every directory entry maps to its family root (`p1.jsonl.2` roots at
`p1.jsonl`), and the deduplicated root set is walked, so each generation is
read exactly once, including a fully rotated family whose current file is
absent.

The collected lines merge ordered by their `ts` field (missing/unparseable
sorts oldest) and the walk keeps the last `replayTailLines` lines (default 2000) globally. Last-wins folds are per-sessionID, and each sessionID's
rows live in exactly one file, so cross-file ordering cannot change any
per-session fold; the global `ts` sort only preserves the observe-mode
global totals' last-wins behavior.

The global slice is also an inclusion bound. Each session-sink family is
read with the full `replayTailLines` window, but the slice keeps the last
window overall: with a hot shared journal plus many session sinks, a quiet
session's entire contribution can fall outside the kept tail, so its boot
gate restore silently fails toward strict (the same eviction spirit as
journal rotation). The merge also bounds boot memory, not just boot I/O:
all read lines are held at once, O((1 + number of session-sink families) ×
`replayTailLines`) lines in the worst case (a bound, not a steady-state
cost). Per-file reads stay tail-capped with an early stop: the walk ends
inside the newest generation that alone satisfies the tail bound, so boot
I/O stays bounded by the retained-generation sizes, never the full
`journalMaxGenerations × journalMaxBytes` envelope (the file count grows
with live sessions; see [the retention note](rotation.md)).

The journal is treated as untrusted data on the read side. A line folds
into the last-wins maps only if its `sessionID` passes the replay ID-shape
check (alphanumeric plus `.`, `_`, `-`, length 1–64) and its kind fields
pass their shape guards: verdict marker ≤ 512 chars, ensemble count an
integer in `[0, REVIEW_ENSEMBLE_SIZE]` (higher integers clamp, others
drop). Each dropped line journals one replay-drop `suppressed` entry
([entry-type catalog](entry-types.md)). An unreadable generation file (a directory in its place, a
permission failure) folds nothing from its lines: it journals one
message-free `{ts, type:"replay", error:true}` entry on the shared
`turnstile.jsonl` (bounded by the generation count) and the walk continues
with the next-older generation.

The walk then restores per session, last-wins: `hasGatePass`,
`hasPlanVerdict` (+ `plansSignature`), `hasReviewApprove` (task-result
source only; streamed child verdicts never restore it), ensemble counts,
the observe period (per-session phase, the admission dedup set, and the
running `observed`/`wouldBlocks` totals; last-wins, and a `kind:"summary"`
marker sets the pending-summary probe), and the gate suspension map
(last-wins `action:"off"` / `action:"on"`; a restart mid-suspension stays
suspended; the `refused:true` refusal flavor and the `event:"would-block"`
audit flavor fold inert).

A plan APPROVE entry may carry the bound identity fields `plan` (file
name) and `planKey` (that file's content hash); a field restores it only
in legal shape (path-free file name ≤ 128 chars; `planKey` a 64-char
lowercase sha256 hex; `plansSig` ≤ 4096 chars). Absent, non-string, or
malformed-shape means unbound, so legacy lines replay unchanged and
hostile bytes degrade to the existing unbound validation paths. Restored
buckets get `replayGrace`, surviving exactly the resume prompt. Values,
not provenance, are carried: a live `GATE: FAIL` after replay stays false.

Staleness then applies per approval kind. A restored _bound_ verdict is
validated against the current files immediately (bound plan edited or
removed → `plan-edited` / `plan-missing` STALE, no accept-once window). A
restored unbound verdict carries its journaled `plansSig` stamp and is
validated against the current dir (any plans-dir change →
`signature-mismatch` STALE). A field-less legacy line keeps the accept-once
window (accepted once and re-stamped). Any read error is fail-open. The
window bounds only the live approval: bound approvals older than it stay
exempt through [the durable approved-plan store](file-layout.md).

For a read-only status view: `opencode-turnstile status [--json]`
aggregates gate/plan/verdict/dispatch/blocked/permission/suspension entries
per parent session, walking the same all-generation tail window with the
same session-ID and marker shape checks (observation-only, so a dropped
line is silent there rather than journaled). Suspension folds last-wins
like the ledger's `foldSuspended` (an OFF marks, an ON clears, a
`refused:true` refusal, an `event:"would-block"` audit, and an unknown
action fold nothing) and surfaces per session as the `suspended` JSON
field and the table's SUS column. When the journal holds observe-mode
entries, the report header adds the folded period line
(`observe: <phase> <observed>/<observeSessions> sessions, <wouldBlocks>
would-blocks`); journals without them render byte-identically. When the
journal holds `plan-rekey` rows (the durable-store scheme migration in the
[entry-type catalog](entry-types.md)),
one advisory line naming the re-keyed plans (capped at five, `+N more`
beyond) renders under the observe line; journals without them render
byte-identically too.

`opencode-turnstile evidence [--task <session|latest>]` is the publishable
half of that view: the same tail window and shape checks, folded to one
task and projected key by key into `turnstile-evidence/v1`: derived
counts, canonical marker lines, and two shas (a one-way task handle, and
`sha256` of the last journaled line). Nothing is filtered out of a larger
object: the document is built from whitelisted keys, so a journal field
cannot leak into a public artifact by oversight. It adds no entry type,
changes no replay rule, and writes nothing to the journal.

# Journal rotation and per-session sinks

## Rotation

The journaler appends on the hot path without stat or rename: `journal()`
only appends and advances a per-file counter. The rotate-then-rename
sequence runs once per `journalRotateEveryEntries` appends (default 512),
only under a created `<file>.lock` atomic-mkdir mutex, so two concurrent
sessions never both rename the shared file. Disk usage stays bounded at
`(N + 1) × maxBytes`, plus at most `journalRotateEveryEntries × ~2 KB` of
overshoot between the size check and the rename. A contended lock or any
rotation error is swallowed (fail-open). The journaler steals a leftover
`<file>.lock` from a crash once its mtime passes the staleness bound
(journaling a `rotation-lock-stale:` `error` entry), so rotation resumes
instead of stopping forever; a freshly held lock is still skipped silently
while journaling keeps appending. One bounded race remains: a writer that
opens the path across the rename may land an entry in a generation past the
current file, but the replay scan walks all retained generations, so such
an entry simply joins the tail window when it is read back (the window is
small and clock-free). Files rotate at 5 MB, 5 generations.

## Per-session sink rules

Each `sessions/<parentID>.jsonl` file carries the same rotation bounds as
the shared file (5 MB, 5 generations, same lock cadence and stale-lock
steal). The steal's `rotation-lock-stale:` error row always appends to the
shared `turnstile.jsonl`, even when the contended file is a session sink.
Aggregate retention and boot read cost scale with the live session count:
per-file bounds are equivalent, but the file count grows with sessions
(accepted; the shared-file bound alone is unchanged).

### A failing run (illustrative)

A real failing run was not captured for this doc, so this shape is
illustrative. A diverged cell prints its first
divergence as a line diff over the stable serializations, then the removal
lines, then a summary that names the failed scenarios.

An example is shown below:

```text
## replay: FAIL (cells=7)
--- ref replay.refused-approve
+++ HEAD replay.refused-approve
-{"drops":0,"sessions":{"p1":{"hasReviewApprove":false,…
+{"drops":0,"sessions":{"p1":{"hasReviewApprove":true,…
REMOVED-IN-HEAD: replay.recovery-row
DIFFERENTIAL: FAIL scenarios=6 cells=875 failed=1 skipped=1 newInHead=68 [replay(2)]
```

`--- ref <cell>` / `+++ HEAD <cell>` name the cell and the two trees; `-`
lines exist only in the ref, `+` lines only in HEAD. `REMOVED-IN-HEAD:` is a
cell the ref had and HEAD lost. The trailing `[replay(2)]` names each failed
scenario with its diverged-plus-removed cell count. The command exits 1.

### Drift-tolerance rules

All four live in `scripts/differential.mjs`; know them before reading a run
as a verdict:

- **Skip on absent in ref.** A scenario whose driver needs a module the ref
  tree lacks reports `SKIPPED (absent in ref)` instead of crashing.
- **Growth is non-failing.** Cells present only in HEAD print
  `NEW-IN-HEAD:` and count toward `newInHead=`, but didn't fail the run.
- **Removal and divergence fail.** A cell present only in the ref
  (`REMOVED-IN-HEAD:`) or holding a different value (the `--- ref`/`+++ HEAD`
  diff) fails its scenario.
- **Re-point after a deliberate change.** When you change behavior on purpose,
  point `--ref` at the commit that introduced the change.

# Field-tested on itself

Turnstile is built with turnstile: most of this plugin's own development
runs through the pipeline it enforces, gates and journal on, so the
enforcement doubles as a field test. In the first week of that (Oct 8–15,
2026), the journal records ~350 pipeline dispatches and ~390 blocked calls
on this repo. Most of those blocks are the read-horizon cap doing its
unglamorous job; about 65 caught real pipeline violations: executor
dispatches without an approved plan, unverified `GATE: PASS` claims, invalid
commit subjects, and unapproved pushes that never landed.

This repo now runs the landing gate enforced: an unapproved push is
refused, not journaled. The flip was motivated by 54
`no-landing-approval` would-blocks across 38 sessions — pushes the
approved ensemble had actually earned, recorded by the observe-mode
journaling that predates enforced landing. A fix to
the delivery-credit path (a reviewer `VERDICT: APPROVE` delivered without
`input.agent` never credited the gate) landed before the flip, so the
enforced gate releases on approvals it would otherwise have missed.

Don't take this section at face value: run `npx opencode-turnstile status`
and read the journal yourself.

Publishing that record is part of the field test: this repo ships the
evidence workflow under `.github/workflows`, so the pipeline claims a
reviewer would otherwise take on faith are posted on the pull request
itself — the same artifact the `evidence` command emits, validated in the
untrusted job and published from the base-context one.

# Files and journals

- Journals live outside the repo in `~/.local/share/opencode/metrics/`:
  - `turnstile.jsonl`: shared JSONL audit trail (the fallback sink for
    entries without a sessionID); hot path is append-only and rotates
    once per `journalRotateEveryEntries` (default 512) writes under a
    lock-guarded rename, keeps `journalMaxGenerations` (default 5)
    generations; a lock left behind by a crash between create and remove of
    `<file>.lock` is stolen once its age passes a staleness bound
    (`ROTATION_LOCK_STALE_MS`, 60s) and the rotation proceeds, and journaling
    keeps appending through fresh contention
  - `sessions/<parentID>.jsonl`: per-parent-session segments (when
    `journalPerSession` is on, the default) — every entry with a resolvable
    parent sessionID appends here, so one session's story reads
    top-to-bottom; same rotation bounds per file. Grep one session's
    history with `rg … ~/.local/share/opencode/metrics/sessions/<parentID>.jsonl`
  - `gate-events.log`: human-readable
    `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM | agent | event | detail` lines, with an optional
    trailing ` | <sessionID>` segment when the trace line is wired to a
    session (the first four segments are unchanged when it is absent);
    suppressed entirely by `trace: false`
  - `approved-plans.jsonl`: durable, bounded, project-scoped store of
    bound plan-reviewer approvals (plan name + content key + project
    scope + key-scheme tag (`scheme: "spec"`; untagged = legacy whole-file
    key)), capped at 256 records and rewritten on eviction. A plan whose
    name and content key still match a record for the current project is
    not _pending_ — the plan gate stays green for it even after its
    journal APPROVE line has aged out of `replayTailLines` and across
    prompt resets; an edited or replaced plan (key mismatch) stays
    pending. A legacy record whose whole-file key still matches the
    whole-file sha256 at the current plans scan is honored and re-keyed to
    the spec scheme on first touch (journaled `plan-rekey`; the re-key
    writes the current spec key). A cached scan may reflect the bytes at
    its last refresh rather than the current file — a progress-only edit
    leaves the spec region (and the cached scan signature) unchanged, so a
    legacy record can be honored across such an edit. A record matching
    neither key blocks with
    the `durable-key-stale` reason and a one-re-approval recovery message.
    Fail-open: read/write errors are journaled and the gate
    degrades to journal-replay semantics
- Retention is bounded: 2 files × (1 current + 5 generations) × 5 MB ≈
  ~30 MB per journal, worst case ~60 MB total, plus the approved-plan
  sidecar (≤ 256 short records). With `journalPerSession` on, each live
  session adds its own `sessions/<parentID>.jsonl` with the same per-file
  bounds, so aggregate retention and boot replay read cost scale with the
  live session count. Rotate overshoot is another
  `journalRotateEveryEntries` (default 512) entries × ~2 KB per journal,
  taken between the size check and the rename on the lock tick.
- `.opencode/plans/*.md` containing `## Decomposition` are load-bearing:
  their presence activates the executor chunk-citation gate.
- The journal also carries `{type:"ensemble", sessionID, agent, count}`
  entries: one per unwaived `task -> reviewer` dispatch, carrying the
  running `count`. Under `reviewEnsemble: enforce`, declining a
  single-reviewer APPROVE adds a `refusedApprove:true` stamp to the last
  `ensemble` entry and a `blocked` entry (`reason:"ensemble-incomplete"`,
  carrying `count` and `need: 2`). A human `always` release journals
  `refusedApprove:false` to clear the stamp. Each type is replayed at boot
  and contributes to the `replayTailLines` tail (default 2000): the last
  `ensemble` entry per session sets `reviewerDispatches`, and when it is
  stamped `refusedApprove:true` replay does not re-credit that APPROVE's
  `hasReviewApprove` on restart. When the landing gate is already released,
  a later APPROVE delivery is credited without a stamp: the release (human
  grant or mechanical) is never re-stamped as a refusal.

# Installing and maintaining

Three ways to install; pick one, and do not combine the plugin-array path
with the CLI install.

1. **Zero-config enforcement (plugin only).** Add the package to your
   OpenCode config's plugin array and restart:

   ```json
   { "plugins": ["opencode-turnstile"] }
   ```

   turnstile loads and enforces its gates, injecting the orchestrator policy
   into the parent session at runtime — nothing is written to any
   instructions file. The pipeline agent definitions are not installed by
   this option alone (recognition is by dispatch _name_, not by installed
   files, so the gates still fire).

2. **Full install via the CLI.** `npx opencode-turnstile init` installs the
   plugin and the pipeline agent definitions into `~/.config/opencode`
   (`plugins`, `agents`, `skills`).

3. **Develop from a clone.** Clone this repo and run `npm run init`
   (symlink mode) so installed artifacts stay live against your edits.

### No postinstall

Turnstile has **no** npm lifecycle hook (`postinstall`, etc.). Installing
`opencode-turnstile` as a dependency never writes to `~/.config/opencode`;
it only makes the gates available through the plugin array. Everything else
(the agent definitions) happens only when you run an explicit command. This
is deliberate: writes to your config directory are opt-in, not automatic.

### Modes

`init` auto-detects an install mode: a git checkout installs by linking (the
working tree stays the source of truth, so edits are live); an `npx` package
install copies files (the installed files are the source of truth). Override
with `--link` or `--copy`:

```sh
npx opencode-turnstile init --copy
```

Copy mode records the mode it used in the ledger (alongside each entry's
source, hash, and version); symlink mode deletes ledger entries rather than
recording them. `check` does not read the mode from the ledger — it
re-resolves it on each run from the CLI flag, then the manifest, then
filesystem auto-detection, so it stays consistent across reruns.

### Check

`npx opencode-turnstile check` verifies the installed state against the
manifest and exits 0 (clean) or 1 (drift). A copy install whose recorded
version is older than the published package is reported as a warning
(`check: outdated <dest> (installed X, package Y)`) and does not fail the
check. Running `init` on a content-identical destination refreshes the
recorded version in place (`install: version stamp updated <dest> (was X,
now Y)`), clearing the warning without rewriting any files.

The check is load-aware, not just presence-aware: after the per-entry pass
it dynamically imports every manifest `verify` path (the installed plugin
entry point by default) through a child `node --experimental-strip-types`,
printing `check: loadable <file>` when the whole import graph resolves and
failing with `check: unloadable <file> — <reason>` when it does not.
`init` applies the same probe to what it just installed, so a missing
module tree fails the install that caused it.

### Upgrade

The plugin updates with your dependency manager (`npm update
opencode-turnstile`, or your registry's equivalent). Re-run `check` to see
whether anything is outdated or drifted, then `init` to re-sync only what
changed: `npx opencode-turnstile init --copy` for package installs,
`npm run init -- --copy` from a clone. The injected orchestrator policy
travels with the plugin, so re-syncing the plugin re-supplies it — there is
no separate contract block to re-sync.

### Uninstall

`npx opencode-turnstile uninstall` reverses the install: it removes
ledger-owned copies and repo-owned symlinks and stops injecting the
orchestrator policy. It is idempotent and ownership-aware: files it never
installed (untracked files, symlinks pointing outside the repo) are left
alone, and a second run is a clean no-op. Injected policy is gone the moment
the plugin is unloaded; a legacy contract block once written by hand into
`~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` is not owned by turnstile and is removed
separately — see
[Policy injection](../architecture/policy-injection.md).

### Retired paths

The manifest also carries a `retired` list: destinations turnstile once
installed but no longer ships (for example the old `turnstile-suspend` and
`turnstile-setup` skills, or the command files from when `status` and `log`
were slash commands). `init`, `check`, and `uninstall` sweep these paths on
every run, so upgrading removes the stale installed copies automatically —
repo-owned symlinks (including links whose repo target is gone) and
ledger-owned copies are removed; anything unowned is reported and left
alone. Between the upgrade and the next `init`, `check` (and
`npm run install:check`) reports the drift and exits non-zero.

### From a clone

This repo is the source of truth for what lands in `~/.config/opencode`:
the plugin and the pipeline agent definitions are installed per the manifest
in `install.json`; unowned files in the target directories are never
touched. Two install modes:

A manifest entry may name a directory as its source (the plugin's `src/`
tree ships this way): the directory installs file-by-file — recursive,
sorted — so each file is individually ledger-recorded (copy) or linked
(link), removed by uninstall, and reported by check.

|                           | Symlink (default)                                   | Copy (`--copy`)                                         |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Best for                  | developing turnstile                                | general use, dotfiles repos that reject foreign links   |
| How targets point at repo | symlinks into the checkout                          | real copies                                             |
| After `git pull`          | nothing to do; edits are live on next session start | re-run `npm run init -- --copy` to re-sync              |
| Editing installed files   | edit the repo; links share it                       | edit the repo; user-edited copies conflict on next sync |

```sh
git clone <repo-url> && cd turnstile
npm install              # typescript + @types/node, for typechecking
npm run init             # symlink mode
# or: npm run install:copy
npm run install:check    # verify installed state; exit 1 on drift (gates local CI)
```

A target that differs from the repo is a **conflict**: `install` fails with
a per-path summary. Re-run with `--force` to back the file up
(`<name>.bak.<timestamp>`) and replace it. Conflicts mean:

- symlink mode: a real file (or a link pointing outside the repo) sits at a
  manifest target and differs from the source, typically pre-existing files
  or hand edits.
- copy mode: an installed copy was edited after install (the ledger can tell
  user edits from repo updates), or an untracked real file sits at a target.

Copy mode records everything it installed in
`~/.config/opencode/.turnstile-install.json` (the ledger: destination mapped
to source, content hash, package version, and install mode). The ledger
makes re-syncs safe: repo updates re-copy cleanly and user edits fail
loudly. It also lets the installer remove copies whose manifest entry was
deleted. Deleting the ledger turns every copy into an untracked file the
installer will refuse to touch.

### Set the agents' models

The seven agent definitions in `agents/` ship **without** a `model:`
frontmatter key. Each subagent therefore runs on the model of the session
that dispatched it — OpenCode v2's documented inheritance rule — so there is
nothing to configure for the common case. The `--print-model-config`
printer covers the six pipeline-stage names; the requirements agent
inherits the dispatching session's model and needs no pin.

To pin a specific model per agent, paste a block into
`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (**plural** `agents` is the v2 key; v1
used singular `agent`):

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agents": {
    "planner": { "model": "oMLX/oQ/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-oQ4-mtp" },
    "plan-reviewer": { "model": "oMLX/oQ/GLM-5.3-Flash-oQ4-mtp" },
    "executor": { "model": "oMLX/oQ/Qwen3.8-27B-oQ8-mtp" },
    "test-runner": { "model": "oMLX/oQ/Qwen3.8-27B-oQ8-mtp" },
    "reviewer": { "model": "oMLX/oQ/GLM-5.3-Flash-oQ4-mtp" },
    "debugger": { "model": "oMLX/oQ/GLM-5.3-Flash-oQ4-mtp" },
  },
}
```

This is the author's actual local setup (a self-hosted oMLX engine serving
Qwen and GLM models). Frontier hosted models work the same way — any
`provider/model-id` your OpenCode install lists, e.g.
`anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5` — and are the right choice if your local
models struggle with the executor or reviewer roles.

Model IDs come from `opencode models` and take the form `provider/modelID`,
with an optional `#variant`. Restarts pick the change up. Because the
shipped definitions are silent on `model:`, a pin you add is the only
definition of that model — there is no merge precedence to reason about.

Copy-mode users: after a `git pull` that changes these definitions, re-run
`npm run install:copy` to pick up the new frontmatter. `npm run
install:check` will report `stale` (not `conflict`) until you do.

### Printing a model config

To generate a `{"agents": {…}}` snippet instead of copying the six agent
names by hand, run the printer. It writes nothing — it short-circuits before
any install work, so the ledger, links, and copies are untouched:

```sh
npm run init -- --print-model-config
```

That prints one entry per agent, each defaulting to a placeholder:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "planner": "<provider>/<model-id>",
    "plan-reviewer": "<provider>/<model-id>",
    "executor": "<provider>/<model-id>",
    "test-runner": "<provider>/<model-id>",
    "reviewer": "<provider>/<model-id>",
    "debugger": "<provider>/<model-id>"
  }
}
```

Seed individual agents with repeatable `--model` seeds. A bare
`provider/model` (optionally `#variant`) seeds all six; `name=` seeds one.
Model ids may be multi-segment — providers require interior slashes, e.g.
`oMLX/oQ/GLM-5.3-Flash-oQ4-mtp` — so the model body is everything after the
first slash.

```sh
npm run init -- --print-model-config \
  --model planner=oMLX/oQ/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-oQ4-mtp \
  --model executor=oMLX/oQ/Qwen3.8-27B-oQ8-mtp
```

Add `--validate` to cross-check every concrete seed against
`opencode models` and exit 1 naming a model it does not list; placeholder
seeds are skipped. `--model` and `--validate` are only valid with
`--print-model-config`: given without it, install.mjs prints an actionable
message and exits 2.

Paste the output into `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (see
[Set the agents' models](#set-the-agents-models)).

### Customizing the pipeline agents

The agent definitions are opinionated on purpose: turnstile recognizes and
clamps them by name, and the marker contract in the agent prompts is what
the plugin enforces against. Editing the installed files is therefore not a
supported customization path: symlink installs share the repo file, and copy
installs conflict on the next sync.

Two sanctioned ways to change the pipeline:

- **Bring your own agents.** Add your own agent definitions (any names) to
  `~/.config/opencode/agents/`; the installer never touches files it does
  not own. Then point turnstile at them via
  `~/.config/opencode/turnstile.json`: `agents.planReviewer`,
  `agents.reviewer`, `agents.executor`, `agents.testRunner`, and
  `agents.debugger` take the names turnstile should recognize, clamp, and
  hold to the marker contract. Your agents get the same gates the shipped
  ones do. Gate authority follows these configured names, not the agent's
  role: an agent that runs the test suite under a custom name (e.g. `build`)
  must be configured as `agents.testRunner` — `agents.bareOutput` then
  derives — or its `GATE:` markers are journaled as `suppressed` and the
  gate stays red.
- **Fork the repo.** To change the pipeline content itself, fork and edit
  `agents/*.md` there; your installer serves your fork.

One coupling to know when customizing either way: the shipped definitions
reference `.opencode/plans/` as turnstile's **default** `plansDir`, not a
constant — the plan path travels in the dispatch prompt, and the agents are
instructed to honor it over the default (see the frontmatter comment in
`agents/planner.md`). If you reconfigure `plansDir`,
update your agent definitions' write permission (planner) accordingly; a
copy-mode user edits their installed copies, a fork edits `agents/*.md`.

### Updating

Symlink mode: because everything is linked into the checkout, updating is
just:

```sh
git pull            # in this repo
npm install         # only if dependencies changed
```

then restart OpenCode sessions (or `opencode service restart`) so the
running server reloads the plugin. There is no separate install step for
code or agent changes; the links are already live. Re-run `npm run init`
only when the **set** of artifacts changes (a new agent added to
`install.json`, an artifact removed or moved): it creates, fixes, or removes
repo-owned links to match the manifest.

Copy mode adds one extra step, because copies do not follow the repo:

```sh
git pull            # in this repo
npm install         # only if dependencies changed
npm run init -- --copy   # re-sync: re-copies changed files, skips clean ones
```

then restart OpenCode sessions. Unchanged files are skipped; changed ones
are re-copied; user-edited copies conflict and wait for `--force`.

Shared caveats:

- Symlinks point at the clone's absolute path. Do not move, rename, or
  delete the checkout; if you relocate it, re-run `npm run init`.
- `npm run install:check` reports drift between the manifest and what is
  actually installed. There is no `install:agents:check`: the orchestrator
  policy is injected from code (`src/policy.ts`), not a manifest-managed
  template, so nothing to verify there — `npm run ci:installed` is now just
  `install:check`. These install checks must run after `npm run init` on a
  machine with artifacts installed — a fresh clone has nothing to check. The
  host chain (`npm run ci` = `npm run ci:host`) covers lint, format:check,
  typecheck, check:markers, and test without the install checks. GitHub CI
  runs `npm run ci:host`, the host chain only, because a runner has no
  installs to check. Verify a copy install with
  `npm run install:check -- --copy`.
